chapter: Piano influences: Teddy Wilson, Tatum and Bud Powell
title: Tatum at the whites-only Maryland club on a spinet piano
summary: Malachi sits by the piano at a segregated club where Tatum plays a poor spinet without complaint.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: There was one aspect of Art Tatum coming to Washington that I didn't realize then, but it just brings out some of the things that were happening with Jazz back then, or the Jazz musicians so-called -- the conditions that they worked under. Art Tatum used to come to Washington and play at a club called the Maryland down on M Street between 14th and 15th. It was a White club, and no Blacks were allowed in there. I used to go to work with Art, and he would have me at a chair near the piano where I could sit, I guess so I wouldn't contaminate the customers or something -- I don't know.
Anyway, I think the pathetic thing about it was that Art

played a spinet piano. He was doing the solo then. It was tuned and everything, and I guess at that time it was fairly new. But it was still a spinet, and I think it was probably a Wurlitzer or something like that. It wasn't any kind of a good instrument that you would imagine somebody like Art Tatum playing at all. When you think about it now, when there were... For example, whenever Oscar Peterson or Ahmad Jamal play, it's in their contract to have a decent piano, and most times it's a 9-foot Steinway grand or, in some cases for Oscar, a Bosendorfer.

But Art Tatum went through a lot of things like that, playing all sorts of lousy pianos and everything. And he never seemed to complain at all. A lot of times you didn't know how lousy the piano was until you sat down and tried to play it yourself! Then you realized that it was just something different about the way he did it, that you didn't notice these things when he was playing.
